abstract: Accurate prediction of Marshall Stability (MS) and Marshall Flow (MF), which are key performance parameters of asphalt mixtures, is of critical importance for optimizing pavement characteristics against the economic, environmental, and traffic-related effects associated with binder content, as well as for reducing reliance on laboratory testing. In this study, 375 Marshall asphalt mixture experimental datasets obtained from the General Directorate of Highways of the Republic of Türkiye were utilized. Hybrid machine learning models were developed by combining six predictive methods with nine different variable selection techniques, and performance metrics were evaluated separately for both MS and MF predictions. Statistical analyses of the dataset revealed a high degree of multicollinearity among fundamental parameters, including bulk specific gravity (Dp) (Variance Inflation Factor; VIF = 3106.25), maximum theoretical specific gravity (Dt) (VIF = 3039.09), and air voids (Vh) (VIF = 5455.66). This condition resulted in limited predictive performance of linear regression models (MS: R² = 0.13–0.18; MF: R² ≈ 0.28–0.32). In contrast, tree-based and ensemble models demonstrated high predictive accuracy. The Shapley Additive Explanation Random Forest-Gradient Boosting (SHAP RF–GBoost) model achieved R² = 0.96, RMSE = 33.09, and MAPE = 2.56 for MS prediction, while the Full Model–RF and (Sensitivity Analysis) SA–RF models yielded R² = 0.91 and RMSE = 0.19 for MF prediction. RF models provided a balanced solution between accuracy and computational efficiency, with execution times ranging between 7 and 13 s. Variable importance analysis indicated that binder content (Wa) and Dt are the most influential parameters, whereas mixture temperature (T), voids (Vh), voids in mineral aggregate (VMA), and voids filled with bitumen (Vf) contribute indirectly yet critically to model performance. The findings demonstrate that hybrid modelling and variable selection approaches successfully capture the non-linear behaviour of asphalt mixtures. The proposed method reduces dependence on laboratory testing, offering both time and cost advantages. The GBoost model, using four variables selected by SHAP RF (T, Dt, Vh, Vf), accurately predicts Marshall stability values reported in the literature. While prediction errors range between 1 and 10% for medium and low MS values, higher errors are observed at elevated MS levels. Overall, the results indicate that variable selection enhances model performance. Future studies may improve model reliability and applicability by expanding datasets, incorporating field validation, integrating diverse traffic and environmental conditions into the modelling framework, and further adopting interpretable machine learning techniques such as SHAP.
journal_title: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

title: A Comprehensive Survey on Symbolic Regression: State-of-the-Art Approaches, Key Applications, Benchmark Evaluations, and Future Research Directions
abstract: Abstract Symbolic regression autonomously discovers interpretable mathematical expressions from data by optimizing functional structure and associated parameters. Unlike traditional regression approaches that rely on predefined model forms, symbolic regression generates explicit models that maintain high predictive accuracy while providing valuable scientific insights. This survey comprehensively analyzes contemporary symbolic regression methodologies by systematically integrating four paradigmatic approaches: deterministic methods, metaheuristic algorithms, neural-symbolic frameworks, and emerging hybrid strategies. We establish a unified taxonomic framework that bridges evolutionary computation, mathematical programming, and deep learning paradigms. Our analysis reveals convergence patterns toward physics-informed discovery, multi-objective optimization, and human-collaborative frameworks. WWe examine hybrid integration strategies, semantic-aware operators, and constraint-handling mechanisms, and we critically assess evaluation methodologies, benchmarking practices, applications across scientific and engineering domains, and fundamental limitations, including search complexity, overfitting, and high-dimensional scaling challenges. This work makes four key contributions. First, we provide a unified framework analyzing over 300 methods across four paradigms. Second, we offer comprehensive coverage of developments from 2020 to 2025, including transformer-based and large language model approaches. Third, we present a systematic analysis of hybrid strategies and convergence patterns. Fourth, we provide actionable guidance for method selection. This survey establishes a comprehensive contemporary reference for symbolic regression research, highlighting pathways toward robust, interpretable, and scalable automated scientific discovery systems.
journal_title: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

title: Deterministic Mathematical Models Applied to Forest Fire Phenomena: A Systematic Review
abstract: Predicting the spread of forest fires depends on precise mathematical tools to ensure environmental safety. Deterministic models simulate fire dynamics using continuous differential equations rooted in fluid mechanics and thermodynamics. Changes in landscape heterogeneity and climate conditions demand adaptive frameworks for accurate risk assessment. This systematic review analyses 56 studies published between 2015 and 2025. The PICO strategy and PRISMA protocol guided the literature selection from the Scopus and Web of Science databases. Within this review, deterministic formulations are defined by physical conservation laws. Hybrid architectures, such as neural networks informed by physics, are included only when they preserve this physical core. Within the evaluated models, topography, wind speed, and fuel characteristics frequently emerge as key variables driving macroscopic fire spread. Modern simulators integrate these physical equations with empirical observations to improve spatial accuracy and validate flame temperatures using data from the United States, China, and Russia. Nevertheless, substantial computational limitations persist. Traditional numerical solvers do not accurately parameterise heterogeneous fuels. Meanwhile, neural networks exhibit mathematical convergence issues, high sensitivity to sparse data, high computational costs, and scalability across large spatial domains. To mitigate these limitations, future predictive tools must implement bidirectionally coupled fire-atmosphere systems. These advanced systems merge continuous physical laws with dynamic data assimilation to improve the reliability of predictions.
journal_title: Archives of Computational Methods in Engineering

title: Space–Time Computational Analysis of the Orion Spacecraft Parachute Aerodynamics and Fluid–Structure Interaction: Virtual Test and Evaluation in Parachute Design
abstract: Abstract The Space–Time Computational Flow Analysis (STCFA) enabled the virtual test and evaluation of spacecraft parachutes and helped reach the final design of the parachutes used in the Orion spacecraft landing in April 2026. Computational fluid–structure interaction (FSI) analysis of spacecraft parachutes requires overcoming a number of formidable challenges. (i) Because the parachute dynamics involves very large air masses compared to the parachute structure mass, the coupled fluid and structure equations need to be solved with the most robust coupling method practically realizable. Otherwise, the computation can generate nonphysical parachute-shape fluctuations, which would be mistaken for actual, physical shape fluctuations. That would, of course, throw off the design process if the design objective is to minimize the physical fluctuations. (ii) Spacecraft parachute canopies have a “ringsail” construction, creating a “geometric porosity” with hundreds of ring gaps and sail slits that the flow goes through to enhance the canopy shape stability, making the FSI problem seemingly intractable. (iii) Spacecraft parachutes are typically used in cluster configurations, where the parachute canopies interact with each other, creating flow computation challenges associated with large mesh deformations and contact between moving structural surfaces. (iv) The final parachute design had, beyond the hundreds of gaps and slits, a “modified geometric porosity,” aimed at enhancing the canopy shape stability. In FSI computations with such modified geometric porosity, the flow through the “windows” created by the removal of the panels and the wider gaps created by the removal of the sails has to be represented in a different way than the flow through the gaps and slits, because they are larger and their sizes are design parameters. Together with the core STCFA methods, a number of ancillary methods played an essential role in overcoming these challenges, leading to the first-ever FSI computation of the Orion spacecraft final-design parachute clusters, which was reported in 2013. We provide an overview of the core and ancillary STCFA methods that enabled the computations reported in 2013 and summarize the computations carried out for various parachute designs tried before reaching the final design and for other types of parachutes involved in the deceleration of the Orion spacecraft as it returns to Earth. We also provide an overview of the methods we introduced since 2013 to increase the fidelity and scope of spacecraft parachute computational flow analysis and summarize the computations carried out since then. These new developments include extending the computations to compressible flows and upgrading the discretization from finite elements to isogeometric analysis, first with NURBS and then with T-splines.
